title: Maximum Number of Fish in a Grid
statement:
You are given an `m x n` grid `grid` (0-indexed). A cell holding `0` is land; a cell holding a positive value is water containing that many fish. Two cells are adjacent when they share a side (up, down, left or right).

A fisher picks any water cell to start on. As often as they like, they may take every fish in the cell they stand on, or step to an adjacent **water** cell (never onto land). Return the largest number of fish the fisher can collect with the best choice of starting cell, or `0` when the grid has no water cell.
notes:
## Intuition

From a starting water cell the fisher can reach exactly the water cells connected to it through side-sharing water cells, and can empty every one of them. So the answer is the largest total of fish over all connected groups of water cells, the same idea as finding the biggest island but weighted by the fish counts. A flood fill (DFS) from each unvisited water cell measures one group at a time.

## Approach

1. Make a `visited` matrix of the grid's size, all `false`.
2. `dfs(r, c)` returns `0` when the cell is outside the grid, already visited or land. Otherwise it marks the cell, starts `fish` at the cell's value, and adds the results of the four neighbours.
3. Scan every cell; when it is water and not yet visited, run `dfs` from it and keep the largest total in `best`.
4. Return `best` (it stays `0` if there is no water).

## Example 1, step by step

The scan first meets `(0,1)` with `2` fish; its group is `(0,1)` and `(0,2)`, total `3`, so `best = 3`. Next `(1,0)` and `(2,0)` form a group of `4 + 1 = 5`, so `best = 5`. Then `(1,3)` and `(2,3)` give `3 + 4 = 7`, so `best = 7`. The last group, `(3,1)` and `(3,2)`, sums to `5`. The answer is `7`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): each cell is marked once and checks four neighbours.
- Space: O(m · n) for `visited` and the recursion depth in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Mark a cell as visited before recursing, or two neighbours will keep calling each other forever.
- Only side neighbours count; diagonal water cells belong to different groups.
- Land cells (value `0`) block movement, so never step onto them even to reach more water.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | grid dimensions |
| `visited` | which cells already belong to a measured group |
| `dfs(r, c)` | fish in the not-yet-visited part of the group containing `(r, c)` |
| `fish` | running total inside one `dfs` call |
| `best` | largest group total found so far |

narration.4: Track visited cells so each water cell is counted in exactly one group.
narration.6: Flood fill from (r, c) and return the fish it collects.
narration.7: Stepping outside the grid collects nothing.
narration.8: Land, or a cell already collected, also adds nothing.
narration.9: Mark this water cell before exploring so the search never comes back to it.
narration.10: Take the fish in this cell.
narration.11: Add whatever the search below collects, then above, right and left.
narration.18: Largest catch seen so far; it stays 0 when there is no water.
narration.19: Scan every cell of the grid row by row.
narration.21: A water cell not yet visited starts a new connected group.
narration.22: Measure that whole group with DFS and keep the larger total.
narration.26: Return the richest group of connected water cells.
